prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of work, anchored in the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a vast metaphysical architecture of the novel.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged. The laureate configuration is the same, but I have narrowed the citation after the exchange. On the common criteria, Cărtărescu offers a voice that is hard to confuse with any other, formal and linguistic ambition sustained at very large scale, and imaginative depth that is built from the body, memory and dream into one project. As publicly described, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid are the demonstrated peak. A single-writer, single-language entry makes the credit unambiguous. The chair asked which works should anchor a citation and whether it should name poetry. My answer is that the citation should be tied to the prose that members can actually discuss, and should not claim breadth that no one has assessed. I would let the poetry and essays appear only as context for the coherence of the project. The poetry is not a scope the committee has tested, so naming it would claim more than the evidence supports. I do not count the six-of-six agreement in round 1 as merit. The chair is right that it has not yet been tested against the strongest alternatives, and my position rests on the criteria and on the open questions below. This judgment rests on public knowledge and translated reception, not on a full reading or independent verification.
statement.case_against: The reservations stay the same and are still unresolved. The linguistic achievement, which is central to the claim, is the part I can verify least, because the effect of long, recursive Romanian sentences is not available to me directly. Whether Solenoid and the later novels deepen the project or only extend it remains open. I cannot settle it with book-level evidence, and no member has offered any. Density may be imaginatively necessary, or it may become mannered, and I have no secure criterion for distinguishing the two beyond asking whether each book adds a new structure, image-system or argument and not just more of the same. If that test failed for the later novels, the citation would narrow to the central trilogy, and Adonis's renewal of Arabic poetic language would become the stronger comparison. I cannot judge Adonis's prosody directly either, so the comparison is unequal. That inequality is a limit on my confidence. It is not an argument for either writer.

responses.point: Olsson says the citation should be defined carefully, naming prose and poetry, and not assume the poetry is covered because it appears on the ballot. He also treats Adonis as the strongest competing case, and says the committee's own competence in Arabic is uncertain.
responses.response: I agree on the need for care, and I draw the opposite conclusion about wording. A citation that names poetry would credit something the committee has not assessed, so I have anchored mine in Orbitor and Solenoid and removed the claim of poetry. If members with Romanian-language access can vouch for the poetry, it can be added later. On Adonis, I agree that the weakness is competence in Arabic, and I would not close it by relying on age or timing. I would rather ask what the regional expert input you mention can establish about the later poetry compared with the foundational books. Until that is answered, I keep him as my first alternative and do not move him above Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg reads the recurrence of body, memory, dream and cosmology as the project's method and not a failure of invention. He would keep the citation on the sustained inner-cosmos project and not on every late volume. He also argues that translation limits lower confidence about Adonis's prosody but not the documented scale of his reshaping of Arabic poetics.
responses.response: I accept the practical conclusion, which is to cite the project and not every volume. I would add a test for his reading of recurrence as method. The recurrence is method if each volume changes its structure or scale. It is a weakness if only the motifs return. That is something members could cite book by book, and I do not think we have done so yet. On Adonis, I agree that translation limits confidence in sound and diction without erasing documented historical significance. I would add that documented significance is itself partly reception and not a firsthand assessment of the poems. That is why I keep him a serious alternative but not my first choice.

responses.point: Mattson says the fair test is whether density stays purposeful across the full length of the major novels or sometimes becomes accumulative. She would resist letting that doubt push the committee toward a more compact but narrower body of work.
responses.response: I agree that we should not trade a singular large project for a safer small one just because the large one is harder to verify. I would still keep the doubt explicit in the citation scope. That is the reason I have named Orbitor and Solenoid as the anchor and not the whole corpus equally. The citation can be ambitious about what it names while staying modest about what it covers. I think that answers both your caution about scope and your resistance to narrowness.

responses.point: Palm says she would revise her seventh-place ranking of Zurita upward if the committee could establish that the printed poems carry the achievement alone. She says subject, such as the context of dictatorship, cannot fill that gap.
responses.response: I ranked Zurita fifth for similar reasons and would give the same answer. If the printed sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, are shown to stand on language and form in the Spanish text, my ranking could rise. Even then, I do not know that I would place him above Cărtărescu, because his cumulative, visually structured poems are especially exposed to translation loss. That is a statement about the evidence available to me. It is not a claim that the poems are weaker. I agree with you that the historical context cannot substitute for evidence on the poems themselves.

uncertainties: Translation: Cărtărescu's Romanian syntax, rhythm and density cannot be verified by me directly. The same limit applies to Adonis's Arabic prosody and Zurita's Spanish sequences, and the three limits are unequal and not resolved.
Sustained quality: I have no book-level evidence on whether Solenoid and the later novels extend the project of the Orbitor trilogy or repeat it.

Corpus coverage: the poetry, early work and essays are thinly covered, so I have kept them out of the citation's scope. Whether the committee has access to reliable Romanian-language readings of them is unknown.
Hybrid, visual and landscape-scale works (Carson, Zurita) raise open questions under the will's phrase 'literary works'.

Whether a co-opted member's vote counts is undocumented. The weight of my simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and this round-2 recommendation models a committee recommendation and not the Academy's decision.
I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer. My assessments rest on public knowledge and translated reception.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1, and none apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records professional ties to colleagues (election alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020, work with chair Anders Olsson, marriage to Pär Nuder) and my biography of Alfred Nobel. None of these connects to a shortlisted writer. My non-fiction practice is context and not evidence of a preference. My role as Permanent Secretary does not give me any documented link to a shortlisted writer. I have not recorded a conflict and none is adjudicated here.
